festivals.description: This major festival marked the completion of a full Aztec calendrical cycle. All fires were extinguished, and a new fire was kindled on the chest of a sacrificial victim, symbolizing the renewal of the sun's power and the continuation of the world.

festivals.name: Panquetzaliztli
festivals.description: Although primarily dedicated to Huitzilopochtli, this festival also involved honoring the sun. It included feasts, dances, and the presentation of offerings to both deities.

cultural.modernLegacy: While direct worship of Tonatiuh ceased with the Spanish conquest, his image remains a powerful symbol of Aztec identity and heritage. He is often depicted in art, literature, and popular culture as a representation of the sun's life-giving energy and the strength of the Aztec empire. Representations of Tonatiuh are also found in modern Mexican cultural symbols.

worshipPractices.name: Human Sacrifice
worshipPractices.description: The most significant form of worship was human sacrifice, believed necessary to nourish Tonatiuh and ensure the sun's continued movement. Warriors, especially those captured in battle, were often offered as sacrifices.

worshipPractices.name: Ritual Offerings
worshipPractices.description: Offerings of food, animals, and precious objects were made to Tonatiuh. These offerings were intended to appease the god and ensure his continued favor.

worshipPractices.name: Sun Dances
worshipPractices.description: Elaborate sun dances and ceremonies were performed to honor Tonatiuh and celebrate the sun's power. These ceremonies often involved music, dancing, and feasting.

description: Tonatiuh, in Aztec mythology, was the sun god of the Aztec empire. He was considered the leader of Tollan and the fifth and current sun. According to the Aztec creation myth, the world had gone through four previous suns, each destroyed by cataclysm. Tonatiuh demanded human sacrifice to sustain him and ensure the sun's daily journey across the sky. Without this nourishment, the sun would fail to rise, plunging the world into eternal darkness. He is often depicted as a fierce warrior, adorned with eagle feathers and holding a shield. His face is typically red, symbolizing the heat and energy of the sun. Tonatiuh's role was crucial for the survival of the Aztec people, as he provided light, warmth, and life-giving energy. He was closely associated with warfare and sacrifice, reflecting the Aztec belief that human blood was necessary to maintain cosmic order. The god's image was prominently featured on the Aztec calendar stone, emphasizing his central importance in their cosmology. Tonatiuh was believed to reside in the heavens during the day and journey through the underworld at night, battling forces of darkness before emerging again at dawn. He embodies the cyclical nature of life, death, and rebirth, and is a powerful symbol of the Aztec worldview.
subtitle: The Aztec Sun God of the Fifth Sun

keyMyths.title: The Fifth Sun
keyMyths.description: Tonatiuh became the fifth sun after Nanahuatzin sacrificed himself in a fire. This act brought light to the world, initiating the current era.

keyMyths.title: Daily Journey
keyMyths.description: Tonatiuh traverses the sky each day, requiring human blood to maintain his strength. Without sacrifice, he would fail and the world would end.

keyMyths.title: Underworld Passage
keyMyths.description: At night, Tonatiuh journeys through the underworld, battling forces of darkness. This journey is perilous and requires assistance from other deities.

shortDescription: Tonatiuh was the Aztec sun god and leader of Tollan, the fifth and current sun. He required human sacrifice to sustain his daily journey across the sky.
name: Tonatiuh

extendedContent.title: Origins & Birth
extendedContent.content: In Aztec cosmology, Tonatiuh represents the fifth and current sun, also known as Nahui-Ollin, the Sun of Movement. According to the Aztec creation myth, the world had previously been ruled by four other suns, each destroyed by a different cataclysm. The gods gathered in Teotihuacan to decide who would become the new sun. Nanahuatzin, a humble and diseased god, and Tecuciztecatl, a proud and wealthy god, volunteered. Nanahuatzin bravely leapt into a sacrificial fire and emerged as Tonatiuh, the radiant sun. Tecuciztecatl hesitated and then followed, becoming the moon, but his light was dimmed as punishment for his lack of courage. This myth highlights the importance of sacrifice and humility in the Aztec worldview and explains the origin of the sun and moon.

extendedContent.title: Major Myths & Stories
extendedContent.content: Tonatiuh's primary myth revolves around his daily journey across the sky. The Aztecs believed that he was a warrior who fought each night to overcome the forces of darkness. He was carried across the sky each day by the souls of fallen warriors and women who died in childbirth, who were considered to be equally courageous. At sunset, he entered the underworld, Mictlan, where he battled the forces of darkness before being reborn each morning. This constant struggle required sustenance, which the Aztecs believed was provided by human sacrifice. The myth of Tonatiuh underscores the Aztec belief in the cyclical nature of time, the importance of sacrifice, and the constant battle between opposing forces.

extendedContent.title: Worship & Cult
extendedContent.content: The worship of Tonatiuh was central to Aztec religious life. Temples were dedicated to him, and priests conducted elaborate rituals to ensure his continued favor. The most significant aspect of his worship was human sacrifice, believed necessary to provide him with the energy to continue his daily journey. The hearts of sacrificial victims were offered to Tonatiuh, symbolizing the transfer of life force. Captives taken in war were considered the most suitable sacrifices, as their deaths honored both Tonatiuh and the Aztec state. Festivals were held in his honor, featuring music, dance, and the presentation of offerings. The priests played a crucial role in interpreting the will of Tonatiuh and ensuring the proper performance of rituals.

extendedContent.title: Legacy & Influence
extendedContent.content: Although the Aztec empire fell to the Spanish in the 16th century, Tonatiuh continues to hold a significant place in Mexican culture and identity. His image is often used to represent the Aztec civilization and its rich history. Depictions of Tonatiuh can be found in art, literature, and popular culture. The most famous representation is the Sun Stone, also known as the Aztec calendar stone, which features Tonatiuh's face at its center. This iconic artifact serves as a powerful symbol of Aztec cosmology and artistic achievement. The legacy of Tonatiuh reminds us of the complex religious beliefs and cultural achievements of the Aztec people.

festivals.name: Hueytozoztli
festivals.description: The festival of Hueytozoztli was dedicated to Xilonen and other earth goddesses. It involved processions, dances, and the offering of flowers and food to ensure a successful maize harvest. The festival celebrated the growth of the young maize plants.

festivals.name: Xilonen's Feast
festivals.description: A feast was held at harvest time to celebrate Xilonen's bounty. The first fruits of the maize harvest were offered to the goddess, and communal meals were shared to give thanks for the sustenance provided.

cultural.modernLegacy: While not actively worshipped, Xilonen's legacy persists in Mexican agricultural traditions and cultural memory. She represents the vital importance of maize and the earth's life-giving power.

worshipPractices.name: Offerings of Maize
worshipPractices.description: Offerings of young maize, tamales, and other food items were common in Xilonen's worship. These offerings symbolized gratitude for her bounty and a plea for continued sustenance.

worshipPractices.name: Sacrifices
worshipPractices.description: In some accounts, ritual sacrifices, possibly including human sacrifices (though debated), were performed to honor Xilonen and ensure the continued fertility of the land. These sacrifices were seen as a necessary exchange to maintain cosmic balance.

shortDescription: Aztec goddess of young maize. Embodiment of sustenance and agriculture, ensuring bountiful harvests.

extendedContent.title: Origins & Birth
extendedContent.content: Xilonen's origins are deeply rooted in the agricultural beliefs of pre-Columbian Mesoamerica. As an embodiment of young maize, her emergence is intertwined with the domestication and cultivation of corn, a staple crop for numerous civilizations in the region. She is closely associated with Chicomecóatl, sometimes considered an aspect of the same goddess or a sister deity, representing mature maize. Xilonen's birth is not described in specific myths, but rather she emerges as a personification of the tender, young corn cob, filled with the potential for nourishment and life. Her existence highlights the Aztec's deep connection to the land and their reverence for the processes that sustain them. She embodies the promise of a successful harvest and the continuation of life through agriculture. As such, she was a critically important deity.

extendedContent.title: Major Myths & Stories
extendedContent.content: While Xilonen does not feature prominently in elaborate narratives like some other Aztec deities, her significance is expressed through rituals and symbolic representations. Stories about her focus on her role in ensuring agricultural abundance. Myths often emphasize the importance of honoring her through offerings and sacrifices to guarantee a plentiful harvest. It was believed that neglecting her would result in famine and hardship. Xilonen's connection to Chicomecóatl further enriches her mythical context. Together, they represent the complete cycle of maize cultivation, from the tender young shoots to the mature, harvested corn. These stories underscore the Aztec worldview, which saw the natural world as imbued with divine power and requiring human interaction to maintain balance and ensure prosperity.

extendedContent.title: Worship & Cult
extendedContent.content: Xilonen's worship was integral to Aztec agricultural practices. Temples and shrines were dedicated to her, where priests and priestesses performed rituals to ensure a successful harvest. Offerings of maize, flowers, and other agricultural products were common, demonstrating gratitude for her bounty. Some accounts suggest that human sacrifices were also made to Xilonen, especially during times of drought or famine, but these practices are debated among scholars. The festival of Hueytozoztli was particularly important, celebrating the growth of young maize and honoring Xilonen and other earth goddesses. The rituals involved processions, dances, and the presentation of offerings. Xilonen's cult highlights the Aztec's profound dependence on agriculture and their belief in the power of ritual to influence the natural world.

extendedContent.title: Legacy & Influence
extendedContent.content: Although the Aztec empire fell to the Spanish conquistadors, Xilonen's influence can still be traced in modern Mexican culture. While direct worship has ceased, the importance of maize remains deeply embedded in the country's cuisine and traditions. Xilonen serves as a reminder of the vital role that agriculture played in Aztec society and the reverence they held for the earth's life-giving powers. Her image and symbolism sometimes appear in contemporary art and cultural expressions, reflecting a continued connection to the Aztec heritage. Furthermore, the ecological awareness and sustainable farming practices promoted by some indigenous communities echo the values associated with Xilonen, emphasizing the importance of respecting and nurturing the natural world for the benefit of future generations. Her legacy is a testament to the enduring power of cultural symbols and the enduring connection between humans and the land.

description: Xilonen, also known as Chicomecóatl ('Seven Serpent'), was a major Aztec goddess associated with young maize, sustenance, and agriculture. She was a vital figure in the Aztec pantheon, representing the life-giving power of the earth and the promise of a bountiful harvest. Her name, Xilonen, translates to 'tender maize cob,' directly linking her to the young, unripe corn that formed a crucial part of the Aztec diet. As Chicomecóatl, she was also linked to the number seven, a sacred number in Aztec cosmology often associated with abundance and fertility. Xilonen was venerated during the Huey Tozoztli festival, a time dedicated to seeking a good harvest. Offerings, including food and sacrifices, were made to her to ensure the continued growth and prosperity of the maize crop. She was often depicted with red paint on her face and carrying ears of corn, symbolizing her role as the provider of sustenance. Xilonen's importance stemmed from the central role of maize in Aztec society and culture. She embodied the hope for a successful harvest and the continuation of life, making her a beloved and respected deity. Her influence extended beyond agriculture, encompassing themes of motherhood, nourishment, and the cyclical nature of life and death. She ensured the continuation of the Aztec people through the provision of food and sustenance. Temples were built in her honor, and elaborate rituals were performed to appease her and secure her blessings. Xilonen was a powerful symbol of fertility and the life-sustaining power of the earth.

keyMyths.title: The Gift of Maize
keyMyths.description: Xilonen, through her divine intervention, ensures a plentiful maize harvest for the Aztec people, preventing famine. This act highlights her role as a benevolent provider.

keyMyths.title: The Seven Serpent Aspect
keyMyths.description: As Chicomecóatl, Xilonen embodies abundance and fertility, represented by the seven serpents. This connection signifies her power over the cyclical nature of life.

keyMyths.title: The Huey Tozoztli Festival
keyMyths.description: During this festival, Xilonen is honored with offerings and rituals to ensure a successful harvest. This event demonstrates the importance of agriculture in Aztec society.

extendedContent.title: Origins & Birth
extendedContent.content: The origins of Xiuhtecuhtli are deeply rooted in the ancient Mesoamerican reverence for fire. As Huehueteotl (Old God), his worship predates the Aztec civilization, with evidence found in Teotihuacan dating back to 200 AD. He embodies the primordial fire, the source of creation and the warmth that sustains life. In Aztec cosmology, Xiuhtecuhtli is associated with the center of the world, the hearth that anchors the universe. He is considered both the father and mother of the gods, representing the duality and generative power of fire. His birth, or rather, his eternal existence, is intertwined with the very beginnings of the cosmos, making him one of the oldest and most fundamental deities in the Aztec pantheon. He represents not just the element of fire, but also the concepts of age, wisdom, and the cyclical nature of existence, reinforcing his importance as a foundational deity.

extendedContent.title: Major Myths & Stories
extendedContent.content: While Xiuhtecuhtli doesn't feature prominently in many standalone myths, his role is crucial in the overarching narrative of Aztec cosmology and creation. He is a key figure in the legend of the Five Suns, the successive eras of creation and destruction. His fire is both a force of annihilation, bringing about the end of one era, and a source of renewal, igniting the new sun and allowing life to flourish again. He is also associated with the creation of humanity, as his warmth and energy were essential for bringing life to the newly formed beings. The New Fire Ceremony, a central ritual in Aztec society, reenacts the myth of cosmic renewal, with Xiuhtecuhtli at its heart. This ceremony ensured the continued existence of the world by ritually rekindling the sacred fire, preventing the descent into darkness and chaos. Thus, Xiuhtecuhtli's story is woven into the very fabric of Aztec belief, representing the eternal cycle of creation, destruction, and rebirth.

extendedContent.title: Worship & Cult
extendedContent.content: The worship of Xiuhtecuhtli was central to Aztec religious life, permeating both public and private rituals. Temples dedicated to him, often adorned with braziers and sacred flames, were focal points for ceremonies and offerings. Priests played a crucial role in maintaining the sacred fires and performing the rituals necessary to appease the deity. Commoners also honored Xiuhtecuhtli in their homes, keeping small fires burning as a symbol of his presence and protection. Human sacrifice was sometimes offered to Xiuhtecuhtli, particularly during the New Fire Ceremony, to ensure the renewal of the cosmos. The victims' hearts were offered to the flames, symbolizing the ultimate sacrifice and the replenishment of the sun's energy. The Izcalli festival, celebrated in his honor, involved feasting, dancing, and the piercing of children's ears, signifying their entry into the community and their connection to the deity of fire and time. The pervasiveness of fire in daily life ensured that Xiuhtecuhtli was a constant presence in the minds and hearts of the Aztec people.

extendedContent.title: Legacy & Influence
extendedContent.content: The legacy of Xiuhtecuhtli extends beyond the decline of the Aztec empire, influencing subsequent cultural and artistic expressions in Mexico. His image as Huehueteotl, the Old God, continues to be a symbol of ancient wisdom and the enduring power of tradition. The concept of cyclical renewal, embodied by Xiuhtecuhtli and the New Fire Ceremony, resonates with modern understandings of ecological balance and the interconnectedness of life. Elements of his iconography, such as the brazier and the wrinkled face, have been incorporated into contemporary art and literature, serving as a reminder of the rich cultural heritage of the Aztec civilization. Furthermore, the reverence for fire as a life-giving and transformative force persists in various indigenous communities, reflecting the enduring influence of Xiuhtecuhtli's ancient worship. His legacy serves as a testament to the enduring power of myth and its ability to shape cultural identity and worldview.

cultural.modernLegacy: While direct worship of Xiuhtecuhtli has ceased, his symbolic representation of fire and time continues to resonate in Mexican culture. Elements of his iconography and the concept of cyclical renewal can be found in art, literature, and cultural celebrations, serving as a reminder of the Aztec worldview and their deep connection to the cosmos.

festivals.name: Izcalli
festivals.timing: The eighteenth month of the Aztec calendar
festivals.description: Dedicated to Xiuhtecuhtli, Izcalli involved rituals of fire and renewal. Children were pierced in the ears, and feasts were held to honor the deity's role in the cyclical passage of time and the promise of a new beginning. It was a time of celebration and reaffirmation of the cosmic order.

festivals.name: New Fire Ceremony
festivals.description: This ceremony involved extinguishing all fires and lighting a new one on the chest of a sacrificial victim. This ritual ensured the continuation of the world and the renewal of the sun. It was the most important festival related to Xiuhtecuhtli.

worshipPractices.name: Fire Offerings
worshipPractices.description: Offerings, including food, precious objects, and even human sacrifices, were burned in sacred fires to appease Xiuhtecuhtli and ensure continued warmth and prosperity. The act of burning was seen as a way to transform earthly goods into divine nourishment.

worshipPractices.name: New Fire Ceremony
worshipPractices.description: The New Fire Ceremony, held every 52 years, was a crucial ritual to prevent the end of the world. All fires were extinguished, and a new fire was kindled on the chest of a sacrificial victim, symbolizing the renewal of time and the continuation of the cosmos under Xiuhtecuhtli's protection.

description: Xiuhtecuhtli, also known as Huehueteotl, was a central deity in Aztec mythology, representing fire, warmth, and the passage of time. He was considered the lord of the year and the patron of rulers, embodying the cyclical nature of life and death. Often depicted as an old man with a wrinkled face, carrying a brazier on his head, Xiuhtecuhtli symbolized ancient wisdom and the enduring power of fire. His role extended beyond mere physical fire; he represented the inner fire of life, the vital energy that sustained all beings. He was also associated with turquoise, a precious stone symbolizing nobility and the divine. Xiuhtecuhtli's festivals involved elaborate rituals and sacrifices, designed to appease the god and ensure continued prosperity and warmth for the people. He was seen as both benevolent and potentially destructive, reflecting the dual nature of fire itself. Offerings made to him included copal incense, food, and sometimes human sacrifices, particularly during the New Fire Ceremony, a crucial event that marked the renewal of the cosmic cycle. He was also linked to the underworld, bridging the gap between the living and the dead. Xiuhtecuhtli's importance is evident in his widespread veneration throughout the Aztec empire, where he was revered as a protector, provider, and a symbol of cosmic order.

keyMyths.title: The New Fire Ceremony
keyMyths.description: Every 52 years, the Aztecs performed the New Fire Ceremony to ensure the sun would rise again. Xiuhtecuhtli played a central role, as the new fire was kindled upon his altar.

keyMyths.title: Xiuhtecuhtli's Age
keyMyths.description: As Huehueteotl, Xiuhtecuhtli is one of the oldest deities, representing the ancient origins of fire and life itself. His age symbolizes wisdom and the enduring nature of the cosmos.

keyMyths.title: Xiuhtecuhtli and the Underworld
keyMyths.description: While primarily associated with fire, Xiuhtecuhtli also had connections to the underworld, acting as a bridge between the realms. This duality reflects the transformative power of fire, both creative and destructive.
keyMyths.source: Histoy of the Indies of New Spain

worshipPractices.name: Sacrifices
worshipPractices.description: Xolotl's worship often involved animal sacrifices, particularly dogs, which were seen as his earthly representatives. Human sacrifices were less common but not unheard of, especially during times of great need or to appease the god's darker aspects.

worshipPractices.name: Ritualistic Games
worshipPractices.description: The Mesoamerican ballgame, Ullamaliztli, was associated with Xolotl. The game symbolized the cosmic struggle between light and darkness, and the players' movements mirrored Xolotl's journey through the underworld. The losers of the game were sometimes sacrificed.

festivals.name: Toxcatl
festivals.timing: During the fifth month of the Aztec calendar
festivals.description: While primarily dedicated to Tezcatlipoca, Toxcatl also acknowledged Xolotl's role as a god of transformation and change. Ritual dances and offerings were made to both deities during this festival.

festivals.name: Xocotl Huetzi
festivals.timing: During the tenth month of the Aztec calendar
festivals.description: This festival, dedicated to the fire god Xiuhtecuhtli, also recognized Xolotl's association with fire and lightning. It involved the raising of a tall pole and a ritualistic competition to climb it, symbolizing the ascent of the sun.

cultural.modernLegacy: Xolotl's image persists in Mexican art, literature, and popular culture, often representing transformation, duality, and the hidden aspects of human nature. He remains a compelling figure in contemporary interpretations of Aztec mythology.

extendedContent.title: Origins & Birth
extendedContent.content: Xolotl's origins are intertwined with the myth of Quetzalcoatl, his twin brother. Born from the virgin goddess Coatlicue, they represent duality – Quetzalcoatl as the feathered serpent of light and wisdom, and Xolotl as the dog-headed god of darkness and transformation. Some accounts say Xolotl was born from a flint knife. His birth was an integral part of the Aztec creation narrative, setting the stage for his crucial role in the subsequent eras of the world. He is often associated with the evening star, Venus, as Quetzalcoatl is with the morning star, further emphasizing their complementary nature. He embodies the concept of the ‘nahual’, a shapeshifting spirit animal closely linked to a person, representing their hidden potential and darker aspects.

extendedContent.title: Major Myths & Stories
extendedContent.content: Xolotl's most significant role lies in the myth of the Fifth Sun. After the previous suns were destroyed, the gods needed to create a new one, but the bones of the previous humans were required. Xolotl accompanied Quetzalcoatl to Mictlan, the underworld, to retrieve these bones from Mictlantecuhtli, the god of death. Despite Mictlantecuhtli's attempts to thwart them, Xolotl and Quetzalcoatl succeeded, though Xolotl was instrumental in escaping, using his cunning and shapeshifting abilities. The bones were then ground and sprinkled with the gods' blood, creating the humans of the Fifth Sun. In another myth, Xolotl, fearing sacrifice, transformed himself into various forms – a young maize plant, a maguey plant with two stalks, and finally, an axolotl (a type of salamander) – before he was eventually captured and sacrificed. This story explains the origin of the axolotl and its connection to the god.

extendedContent.title: Worship & Cult
extendedContent.content: Worship of Xolotl was less widespread than that of other major Aztec deities like Quetzalcoatl or Huitzilopochtli, but it was still significant, particularly in communities that saw themselves as descendants of the earlier, destroyed worlds. His temples were often located on the outskirts of cities, reflecting his association with the margins and the underworld. Priests dedicated to Xolotl performed rituals to appease his darker aspects and to ensure safe passage through times of transition and change. Dogs, considered his earthly representatives, were sometimes sacrificed in his honor. The Mesoamerican ballgame, Ullamaliztli, was also heavily associated with Xolotl, serving as a symbolic reenactment of his journey through the underworld and his struggle against the forces of death.

extendedContent.title: Legacy & Influence
extendedContent.content: Xolotl's legacy extends beyond his specific myths and rituals. He embodies the Aztec understanding of duality, transformation, and the acceptance of the darker aspects of existence. His role as a psychopomp, guiding souls to the afterlife, highlights the importance of death and rebirth in Aztec cosmology. In modern Mexico, Xolotl's image continues to appear in art, literature, and popular culture, often representing the hidden potential within individuals and the transformative power of facing one's fears. The axolotl, his animal form, has become a symbol of Mexico's unique biodiversity and a reminder of the interconnectedness of all living things. Xolotl's enduring presence reflects the continued fascination with Aztec mythology and its relevance to contemporary issues of identity, transformation, and the relationship between life and death.

shortDescription: Aztec god of lightning, death, and transformation. Twin of Quetzalcoatl, he guides souls and represents duality. Often depicted as a dog-headed man.

keyMyths.title: The Creation of Humanity
keyMyths.description: Xolotl helps Quetzalcoatl retrieve the bones of previous humans from Mictlan to create the current generation, demonstrating his vital role in the Aztec creation myth.

keyMyths.title: Xolotl's Sacrifice
keyMyths.description: To set the Fifth Sun in motion, the gods had to sacrifice themselves. Xolotl resisted, transforming into various forms before ultimately succumbing, showing his connection to transformation.
keyMyths.source: Historia de los Mexicanos por sus pinturas

keyMyths.title: Guiding the Dead
keyMyths.description: As a psychopomp, Xolotl guides the souls of the deceased through the perils of Mictlan, the underworld, ensuring their safe passage to the afterlife.

subtitle: God of lightning, dogs, and the underworld.
description: Xolotl, the Aztec god of lightning, fire, death, monsters, misfortune, sickness, and deformities, is often depicted as a dog-headed man or a skeleton. He is the twin brother of Quetzalcoatl, and together they represent duality and transformation. Xolotl played a crucial role in the creation myths, specifically in the Fifth Sun, where he helped Quetzalcoatl retrieve the bones of previous generations from the underworld, Mictlan, to recreate humanity. He is known for his self-sacrificing nature, as he initially resisted being sacrificed to set the sun in motion, transforming himself into various forms like an agave plant, a double corn stalk, and an axolotl to avoid his fate. This association with transformation and duality makes him a complex and intriguing figure in Aztec mythology. He is also considered the psychopomp, guiding the dead on their journey to Mictlan and protecting the sun as it travels through the underworld each night. Xolotl's canine form reflects his connection to the underworld and his role as a guardian, while his association with monsters and deformities highlights the darker aspects of the cosmos and the unpredictable nature of life. His name translates to 'animal', and he embodies the wild, untamed forces of nature. He is a god of transitions, both physical and spiritual, and a reminder of the cyclical nature of existence.
name: Xolotl
